opus-5.5.text:
I think it started when I was quite young, honestly, because in China so much of your life gets reduced to a number. You take the exam, you get a score, and that score decides where you go next. For a long time I just accepted that this was how you measure yourself: rankings, grades, competitions. And I was pretty good at that game, so it felt natural.

But at some point I started asking: okay, after the exam, after the next ranking, after the next offer, what is the score then? There is always another number waiting. If I keep optimizing for whatever metric is in front of me, I'll end up somewhere very local, like a reinforcement learning agent that found a reward hack instead of actually solving the task.

Working in RL made this feel very concrete for me. You learn very quickly that the reward function is everything. If you define it badly, the agent will do exactly what you asked and completely miss what you wanted. So I started thinking: what is my own reward function? If I imagine myself at the very end, looking back, what would I actually care about?

The answer I came to is roughly this: the final score is how much real impact I left on the world, things that keep being useful even when I'm not there anymore. Code that other people build on, ideas that push a field forward, systems that help many people. Not titles, not how much money, not whether people know my name. Those are proxies, and proxies can be gamed.

Once I framed it that way, a lot of decisions became easier. Should I spend time open-sourcing something, writing it cleanly so others can use it? Yes, because that compounds. Should I join a place where the work actually matters at scale, even if it's harder? Yes. It's a long-horizon reward, so you have to be willing to accept some short-term cost.

And I also think it's important to stay honest that I might be wrong about it. Like any reward function, you revisit it. But having one at all, instead of just chasing the next number someone else hands you, that was the real shift for me.

r002.rationale: It defines the final score as lasting real-world impact and explicitly says name recognition is not the measure.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came from a pretty ordinary moment. I was sitting in front of a training dashboard late at night, watching a curve go up, and I caught myself feeling genuinely happy about a number that would mean nothing to anyone outside that room a week later. And I thought, wait, if this is what I'm optimizing for, what's the actual objective? What's the loss function for my whole life?

That framing stuck with me partly because of how I work. In reinforcement learning you're always asking what the reward is, and you learn very quickly that agents will exploit whatever proxy you give them. Citations, titles, how fast your repo gets stars, all of those are proxies. They're correlated with something real, but if you chase them directly you end up a very strange shape of person. So I started asking myself: when I'm old and I look back, what's the metric that I can't game?

For me it ended up being something like, how many people were able to do something they couldn't do before because of a thing I built or explained? That's why I care so much about open source, about writing docs that a student in a random university can actually follow. The first time someone I'd never met emailed me saying they trained their first agent with my code, that counted more than any benchmark. It's not that I stopped caring about scores. I just moved the score to a place where it's harder to cheat.

r001.rationale: The candidate traces the realization to a late-night training dashboard and reflection on optimizing proxies; it does not mention information from Weng’s future self.

r002.rationale: The candidate defines the metric as how many people can do something new because of what Weng built or explained, not how many remember Weng’s name.

astra-6.text:
I think it started with asking myself, whose scoreboard am I using? It’s easy to treat life as a series of things you’re supposed to achieve, without stopping to ask whether those things actually matter to you. And even when you achieve them, there’s always another goal.

So I began to think about it from the other end: if I looked back on my life, what would make me feel that I’d lived it well? I don’t have a final formula. But I think I’d care about the relationships I’d built, whether I’d had the courage to make my own choices, and whether I’d done something meaningful for other people. That shifts how I think about success today.

r002.rationale: It identifies relationships, personal choices, and helping others as measures of a well-lived life, but does not propose that the final score is how many people remember one’s name.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it came from asking myself whose standards I was using. It’s easy to measure your life through things other people can see—your job, your achievements, how successful you appear. But would those things make me feel that I had lived well?

For me, the question became: Did I spend my time on things I cared about? Did I show up for the people I love? Did I have the courage to make my own choices? I’m still figuring it out, but I think the final score has more to do with those questions than with how my life looks from the outside.
